summaries.example: Imagine a cat named Pepper. Pepper can be wet on Monday and dry on Tuesday, but we usually say Pepper is the same cat. Philosophers ask what makes Pepper one thing through these changes. They also ask whether a cat and the part of the cat without its tail could count as one cat or two things.
summaries.summary: Identity is the philosophical idea of being the same. The entry first separates qualitative sameness, which means sharing features, from numerical sameness, which means being one individual. It then studies rules used to understand identity, including Leibniz’s Law: identical things cannot differ in what is true of them. Philosophers ask how we know that something remains the same after changing, such as a person growing or an object losing a part. One view says a continuing object has different parts at different times; another says it is wholly present whenever it exists. Other debates ask whether identity can be relative to a kind, whether a whole is identical with its parts, and whether an identity claim can be vague or only possibly true. Some philosophers, especially David Lewis, argue that identity itself is simple and that the difficult questions are really about objects, persons, language, or possibility.
key_ideas: Identity usually means sameness, but philosophers distinguish being alike from being one and the same individual.
A key rule says that if two things are identical, everything true of one is true of the other. This is often called Leibniz’s Law.
Philosophers disagree about how objects continue through time. Some say an object has different time-parts; others say the whole object is present at each time.
Some philosophers think identity can depend on what kind of thing we are counting, while others defend one absolute idea of identity.
The entry also examines whether identity can be uncertain, whether parts can be identical with a whole, and whether identity itself creates philosophical problems.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use identity whenever we count, name, recognize, compare, or track something through change. Thinking about identity helps us understand why a changed object may still seem to be the same object, why two look-alikes can remain two things, and why words can create puzzles even when the things they name are the same. It also shows how ideas about time, parts, language, and possibility connect.

important_terms.definition: Being the very same thing, not merely being similar to it.
Sameness in qualities, such as color, shape, or kind. Two dogs can be similar in this way without being the very same dog.
Being one and the same individual. A thing has numerical identity with itself, not with a different thing.
A rule or standard for deciding whether two things are the same kind of thing or the same thing over time.
The idea that a thing can stay the same while having different properties at different times.

questions_to_think_about: If a toy changes color and loses a wheel, is it still the same toy? Why?
Can two things look exactly alike and still be two different things?
What should count as the same cat after a tail is removed?
Is being similar enough for counting two things as one?
Are questions about identity really questions about identity, or about what kinds of things exist?

summaries.example: Suppose a statue, Goliath, is made from a lump of clay, Lumpl. At the present time they occupy exactly the same place and have the same material. Yet the clay could survive being reshaped into a ball, while the statue could not remain that statue after such a change. One conclusion is that Goliath and Lumpl are distinct despite coinciding. Another is that their identity is contingent, or depends on how we understand possibility. This case illustrates why material constitution, modal properties, and identity are difficult to separate.
summaries.summary: The entry surveys philosophical disputes about what it means for things to be identical. Numerical identity is normally treated as an absolute relation: each thing is identical with itself and with nothing else. Its central logical principle is Leibniz’s Law, though debates arise over how properties, names, and modal contexts should be understood. Peter Geach challenges the assumption that identity is absolute, proposing that sameness may be relative to a sortal, or kind-term. The entry also examines criteria of identity, including standards for abstract objects and for persistence through time. Endurance treats an object as wholly present at each time, whereas perdurance analyzes it as a collection of temporal parts. Questions about possible worlds lead either to transworld identity or to counterpart theory, which uses similarity rather than strict identity. These views affect debates about contingent identity, such as a statue and its clay, and about vague identity in borderline cases. Finally, the entry considers composition as identity and David Lewis’s claim that identity itself is simple, so apparent identity problems may instead concern personhood, language, parts, or possibility.
key_ideas: Classical numerical identity is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, and is commonly linked to Leibniz’s Law. The converse principle, the identity of indiscernibles, becomes controversial when it concerns only qualitative properties.

Geach argues for relative identity: whether two things are the same may depend on a sortal concept, such as cat or object. The cat-on-the-mat puzzle motivates this view, but several rival solutions are available.
Criteria of identity are not uniform. They may relate objects of one sort to other objects, or directly state when two members of a sort are identical.
Perdurance and endurance offer competing accounts of persistence. Their arguments depend partly on views about temporal parts, properties at times, and modal language.

Cross-world identity creates a problem for changing objects: transitivity seems to conflict with the idea that an object could differ gradually across possible worlds. Counterpart theory uses similarity instead of literal identity.

The debates over contingent identity, composition as identity, and vague identity test whether classical identity can accommodate ordinary judgments about constitution, parts, and borderline cases. Lewis argues that the underlying puzzles may not be problems about identity itself.
summaries.why_it_matters: Identity is built into counting, reference, logic, and ordinary judgments about persistence. Yet apparently simple claims—such as that a changing object remains one object, or that a statue is the same as its material—raise questions about time, properties, language, modality, and ontology. Studying these debates clarifies what different theories are committed to and why no single solution fits every common-sense intuition without a cost.

important_terms.definition: The relation an object has to itself and to no distinct object; unlike similarity, it is not a matter of degree.
The principle that if x is identical with y, every property or truth applying to x also applies to y.
A standard for deciding when objects of a given sort are the same, either at one time or across times.
The view that a persisting object has temporal parts or stages located at different times.
The view that a persisting object is wholly present at each time it exists, though its spatial parts may differ.
The relation of being the same individual in different possible worlds; some philosophers replace it with a weaker similarity relation.
Identity that would be true in some circumstances but not in all circumstances, a possibility debated in connection with rigid names and modal properties.
The thesis that the relation between parts and a whole is closely analogous to identity, or, in its stronger form, literally is identity.

questions_to_think_about: Does Leibniz’s Law support the claim that a statue and its clay are distinct if they have different possible histories?
Does the cat-on-the-mat puzzle establish relative identity, or can one of the alternative solutions explain it better?
Would temporal parts make change easier to explain, or would they conflict with ordinary talk about objects?
Is counterpart similarity a satisfactory replacement for identity across possible worlds?
If a whole is not identical with any one of its parts, in what sense could composition be a kind of identity?

summaries.example: A bicycle can be repaired many times and still be called the same bicycle. But imagine replacing every part, one at a time. When, if ever, does it become a different bicycle? Now imagine possible worlds: in one world it has slightly different parts, and in another it is made from completely different parts. Philosophers ask whether all these bicycles can be the very same bicycle, since identity is usually thought to be transitive: if A is the same as B, and B the same as C, then A should be the same as C.
summaries.summary: Identity concerns being the same thing. The entry distinguishes numerical identity from qualitative similarity: two objects may share many properties without being one object. Classical identity is usually described as a relation each thing has to itself and nothing else, and Leibniz’s Law says that identical things cannot differ in what is true of them. Philosophers still disagree about how identity works in language and how we decide whether things are the same. Geach proposes relative identity, according to which sameness can depend on a kind, such as being the same cat. The entry discusses criteria of identity for numbers, directions, sets, objects, and persons, while noting that these criteria may work in different ways. It then studies identity through change. Endurance says an object is wholly present at different times; perdurance says it has different time-parts. Questions about possible worlds lead to a choice between strict identity across worlds and counterpart theories based on similarity. The entry also considers contingent and vague identity, composition as identity, and Lewis’s view that many apparent identity problems are really problems about other concepts.
key_ideas: Two objects may be qualitatively alike without being numerically identical. Numerical identity is being one thing, not merely resembling another.

Leibniz’s Law supports reasoning from differences: if one thing is square and another is not, they are not identical. But language can make identical things appear different because names and contexts work in special ways.
Geach’s relative-identity proposal says that statements like “the same cat” may not simply mean ordinary absolute identity plus the fact that both objects are cats.
A criterion of identity is a standard for deciding sameness. Philosophers debate whether such criteria define identity, identify kinds of objects, or only give necessary conditions.
Perdurance and endurance disagree about how a thing exists through change. The debate affects puzzles about objects, persons, and temporal parts.
Possible-world cases create pressure for counterpart theory, because similarity can change from one world to another without being transitive in the way identity is.
summaries.why_it_matters: We constantly decide whether something is the same: a friend after growing older, a bicycle after repairs, or a word referring to an object. Philosophical analysis reveals that these ordinary decisions rely on ideas about kinds, parts, time, and possibility. It also teaches us to separate a disagreement about what exists from a disagreement about how language describes it.

important_terms.definition: Being exactly one individual rather than merely sharing features with another individual.
The rule that identical things cannot differ in any genuine property or fact.
A way of deciding whether two things are the same, often for a particular kind of thing such as a number, object, or person.
The view that a continuing object has different temporal parts at different times.
The view that a continuing object is entirely present at each time, even though it can change.
The debated idea that an individual can be the same individual in more than one possible way the world could have been.
A relation of similarity between an object and an alternative version of it, used by some philosophers instead of identity across possible worlds.
The view that sameness may be relative to a kind or sort, such as being the same cat, rather than one absolute relation.

questions_to_think_about: Can two objects have all the same visible features but still be two objects?
What facts should decide whether a repaired bicycle is the same bicycle?
Does a thing need to have all its parts at every time to remain the same thing?
Why might similarity between possible versions be easier to use than identity?
Could a statement be unclear because the word for a kind of thing is vague rather than because identity itself is vague?
